Fagnano III

GeometryTrianglesConstructions
Game: A triangle rolls over its sides and leaves a trail of copies; there is nothing to win or lose.
How to play: Drag the four dots to move the triangle and the dot on its bottom side. Tick the boxes to show the helper lines, the copies, the names or where the dot goes.

Keyboard: Tab to a dot, then use the arrow keys (Shift makes a bigger step).

Look for the math

Fagnano's problem asks for the smallest triangle you can fit inside an acute one. This applet draws Hans Samelson's third proof: roll the triangle over its sides until a short straight line turns into the answer.

Rolling around one corner

Start with ABC. Reflect B in the side CA, then reflect A in the new side B'C, then reflect C in A'B'. Both mirrors pass through C, so the first three triangles share that corner. The side AB and its image A'B' meet at O at an angle of 180° − 2C, so for an acute triangle the two lines are never parallel. Both are the same distance hc from C. The logic test checked this on 441 acute grid triangles and hundreds of random ones; the largest angle error was under 0.01 radians.

The bisector and the midpoint M

Because the two copies of side c are equally far from C, the angle bisector m at O passes through C. Reflect each copy of B in m and take the two midpoints: they are M on AB and M' on A'B'. M is exactly the foot of the altitude from C, MM' is perpendicular to m, and the next copy of M is the reflection of M in M'. Tick "Show construction" to see all three midpoints.

Why this line is the shortest

Take any point P on AB and mark where it lands on the rolled side and on the last copy. The two legs are always equal, and the gap between the first and last copy is a fixed translation. An isosceles triangle with a fixed base is shortest when it flattens, so the broken line is shortest exactly when the three copies of P lie straight — which happens at P = M. The test scanned every hundredth of the side in 441 configurations and found no exception. When the three pieces are folded back, their lengths are the three sides of the orthic triangle, which solves Fagnano's problem.

Where the drawing differs from the text

The page numbers the rolled triangles t1, t2, t3; the applet's own objects start with the original as t0, so its t0 and t2 are the page's t1 and t3. The port keeps the applet's numbering. The applet also rounds a nearly vertical mirror by reflecting across x = A.x instead of the true line; in a handful of drawings this shifts the two legs by about one or two board units, so the "equal legs" and "straight at M" checks allow that much. The claims are meant for acute triangles: pull a corner out and the status line says plainly that they no longer apply.

Tick "Show mapping", then drag P onto the foot of the altitude: the two blue legs straighten into one line. Tick "More triangles" to follow the same pattern further along the strip.
